heading: What to check when a cost segregation report reaches your tax preparer
body:
A completed cost segregation report still needs to be connected to the property’s books and return. Report delivery and tax implementation are separate milestones. Before treating a study as finished, identify who will reconcile the report, evaluate the owner’s tax position, enter any supported changes, and retain the final records.

Reconcile the property and the cost pool

Confirm the property address, ownership, acquisition and improvement history, and the basis used in the study. Compare the report’s total with the supporting closing documents and existing depreciation schedule. Investigate differences before importing component amounts. A detailed classification table cannot resolve an unsupported starting amount.

Ask the preparer to distinguish the property-level analysis from owner-level deduction use. A report may identify shorter-lived components without establishing that the owner can currently use every resulting deduction. Applicable limitations, prior reporting, placed-in-service facts, and the implementation method need separate review.

Assign the handoff responsibilities

The study provider should explain the report and its assumptions. The tax preparer should identify the filing approach and any information needed for the applicable year. The owner should confirm that missing records and outstanding questions have an assigned person and due date. Avoid relying on a promise that everyone will coordinate later.

Retain the final report, reconciliation, preparer’s implementation record, and updated asset schedule together. Include future sale or disposition questions in the planning discussion so accelerated deductions are not evaluated only in the first year. Review IRS Publication 946 with the relevant year’s rules. This learning resource does not replace a property-specific study or professional tax implementation.
